paper_title: OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Action-conditioned world models play a vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-of-view moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, a unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within a single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at a lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on a newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence.

sections.content: Action-conditioned world models play vital role in robotics and autonomous driving, yet existing video diffusion models struggle to maintain dynamic object persistence. When the camera turns away and returns, out-ofview moving entities fail to evolve plausibly in latent space, often mutating or vanishing entirely due to bounded perspective views. To resolve this issue, we propose OmniPersist, unified framework that couples perspective video generation with panoramic evolution within single-stage diffusion model, without relying on auxiliary models or initial panoramic inputs. To maintain efficiency, we model the panoramic stream at lower frame rate, bridging both views across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for temporal aggregation. OmniPersist is agnostic to camera-control architectures, supporting both latent-level and attention-level conditioning. Extensive experiments on newly constructed dynamic benchmark across image-to-video and video continuation tasks demonstrate consistent gains in visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence. 1. Introduction World models [10, 34, 36, 47, 64] aim to predict future states from current observations conditioned on actions, playing an increasingly important role in robotics [20, 52] and autonomous driving [22, 44]. prevalent paradigm generates future videos via diffusion models [3, 26, 39, 54], guided by textual prompts alongside camera trajectories or discrete motion signals, as demonstrated by LingBotWorld [10, 36] and Matrix-Game 3.0 [47]. Despite demonstrating compelling visual fidelity through large-scale training, these models fundamentally struggle to maintain object persistence in dynamic scenes. As result, their visual consistency and motion continuity break down, even causing returning entities to mutate or vanish entirely. We attribute this limitation to both training data biases and fundamental modeling bottlenecks. On the data side, current training data for dynamic scenes heavily favor continuous tracking, rarely featuring scenarios where moving entities exit and subsequently re-enter the cameras field of view (FoV). On the modeling side, vanilla diffusion models are inherently limited in preserving out-of-view dynamics without dedicated constraints and priors. Recent works have recognized this challenge and sought to mitigate it mainly from two perspectives. Some methods utilize retrieval frames [6] and compressed implicit contexts [56] as memory. Others attempt to predict dynamics of specific entity through auxiliary generative models [8] and LLMs [40]. However, the former often recall static appearance cues that fail to reflect continuous natural motion, while the latter introduce heavy system complexity and scale poorly to multientity scenarios. Furthermore, these methods are designed primarily for object consistency across temporal chunks. In fact, even within single video chunk, combining intrawindow bidirectional attention with advanced camera control approaches (e.g., UCPE [60]) remains insufficient to 1 sustain out-of-view dynamic evolution. To address this problem, we propose modeling scene evolution in panoramic space, leveraging complete 360 spatial context to improve the persistence of dynamic world models. This paradigm offers two distinct advantages. First, conceptually, the omnidirectional nature of panoramic space ensures that when an object leaves the camera view, its continuous motion can still be explicitly predicted on global canvas. Moreover, this formulation naturally supports multiple moving objects and inherently preserves background memory, as shown in Fig. 1. Second, practically, panoramic scenes can be represented as standard 2D frames via equirectangular projection (ERP), allowing existing video diffusion foundation models to adapt seamlessly to panoramic data while fully capitalizing on their strong pretrained priors. input. Specifically, we propose OmniPersist, which jointly models the perspective camera view and its panoramic counterpart within single video diffusion model. This unified framework achieves persistent dynamic world modeling in an end-to-end manner, without relying on auxSince generating iliary models or additional dense panorama for every perspective frame introduces heavy computational overhead, we propose to design the panoramic stream to operate at lower frame rate. To effectively bridge these two representations across space and time, we introduce two complementary modules, i.e., Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp). In particular, GeoAnch establishes explicit geometric correspondences between the perspective and panoramic views, enabling direct feature exchange at synchronized timestamps. Meanwhile, TemComp aggregates features across neighboring frames, effectively compensating for the temporal discrepancy caused by the differing frame rates. Concurrently, AlayaVista [33] (within the past two months) also explores panoramic representations, but relies on multi-stage pipeline of panoramic initialization, state evolution, and perspective refinement. In contrast, OmniPersist avoids generating redundant full-rate panoramas, establishing single-stage, unified framework for persistent dynamic world modeling. To ensure broad applicability, OmniPersist is designed to be agnostic to underlying camera-control architectures. We integrate our framework with two representative paradigms, i.e., latent-level trajectory injection via CameraCtrl [11] and attention-level pose conditioning via UCPE [60]. Furthermore, to benchmark dynamic persistence under complex camera movements, we construct paired panoramic perspective dataset featuring diverse trajectory patterns. We systematically evaluate OmniPersist under two settings, namely image-to-video (I2V) generation and video continuation. Extensive experiments across visual quality, camera controllability, revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence demonstrate that our coupled panoramic evolution yields consistent gains across both control mechanisms. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: We propose OmniPersist, single-stage unified framework that jointly generates perspective video and temporally sparse panoramic evolution to improve out-of-view dynamic persistence. We introduce GeoAnch and TemComp to couple dense perspective and sparse panoramic streams through synchronized geometric exchange and neighboring-time feature aggregation. We construct paired panoramicperspective dynamic dataset and demonstrate consistent gains in dynamic persistence and revisit consistency across diverse cameracontrol mechanisms. 2. Related Work Camera-Controlled Video Generation. Camera trajectory control has become an essential capability for interactive world models [10, 34, 36, 47, 64]. Existing efforts encompass text-to-video [1, 46], image-to-video [21, 28, 63], and video re-shooting [2, 35, 57], and roughly (1) Camera-parameter condivide into two paradigms. ditioning directly encodes viewpoints as extrinsic matrices [46], Plücker rays [1, 11], or relative positional embeddings [17, 55, 60]. These representations are used to modulate feature latents via auxiliary branches [1, 11] or inject geometric biases into attention mechanisms [17, 55, 60]. These methods operate strictly within the visible frustum, offering no spatial substrate to sustain the evolution of out-of-view dynamic entities. (2) Explicit 3D reprojection grounds camera trajectories by warping reconstructed 3D geometry into target image or latent spaces. For instance, ViewCrafter [58] and GEN3C [28] condition diffusion on rendered point clouds with iterative scene expansion or 3D caching. MosaicMem [59] retrieves 3D-lifted patches from spatial memory, whereas LSM-World [43] caches 3D latent tokens directly to bypass RGB rendering and re-encoding. However, these approaches rely heavily on external depth estimators and are predominantly restricted to static scenes. In contrast, OmniPersist bypasses 3D reconstruction and provides an omnidirectional canvas that naturally sustains unseen dynamic evolution. It acts as an orthogonal, plugand-play spatial substrate, seamlessly integrating with the camera-parameter conditioning paradigm. Persistent Dynamic World Modeling. World models simulate future states conditioned on current observations and actions. prevalent paradigm generates future videos guided by text and camera trajectories [10, 36, 47, 64]. However, maintaining the evolving states of dynamic outof-view entities remains an unresolved challenge. Existing (1) Memoryapproaches broadly follow three directions. based modeling. HyDRA [6] and MemLearner [56] query 2 or compress historical observations to preserve generation consistency. ReMind [51] employs node-structured curriculum that compels the model to retrieve relevant historical states. While historical memory provides informative anchors, these methods inherently infer unobserved evolution from past evidence, often struggling to sustain continuous visual transitions. (2) Auxiliary entity tracking. LiveWorld [8] uses multiple generative monitors to advance unseen entity states within persistent scene, while WorldDirector [40] employs an LLM to predict object trajectories prior to visual generation. However, relying on external entity-level monitors or LLM planners introduces heavy system overhead, causes pipeline brittleness, and scales poorly to dense, multi-entity interactive scenarios. (3) Panoramic world-state modeling. In concurrent work, AlayaVista [33] first evolves panoramic latent states and then synthesizes perspective observations through viewport rendering and refinement stages. However, it relies on separate panorama initialization stage and incurs high computational costs by predicting full-rate panoramas. In contrast, OmniPersist derives its panoramic conditions directly from the observed perspective prefix and predicts panoramic states at lower temporal rate, establishing single-stage joint diffusion framework. Panoramic Video Generation. Panoramic video generation aims to synthesize temporally coherent 360 content, typically achieved by adapting pretrained perspective video diffusion models. Therein, perspective-to-panorama methods expand input videos while preserving their content and dynamics [19, 24, 48, 50], whereas textand image-conditioned approaches synthesize omnidirectional scenes and motion [9, 42, 49, 50, 61]. Recent methods further extend panoramic synthesis to camera-controlled exploration [18, 32] and 3D world construction [7, 41, 53]. Technically, these methods address spherical distortion and boundary seams through ERP-aware designs [32, 48, 49], cross-view coherence via multi-view attention [9, 50], and exploration consistency through geometric guidance and spatial memory [7, 18, 41, 53]. Collectively, these advances establish the feasibility of using video diffusion models to evolve panoramic states. Unlike prior works targeting standalone panoramic synthesis, OmniPersist couples an efficient, low-rate panoramic stream with perspective rollouts to anchor out-of-view dynamic persistence. 3. Method 3.1. Overview We study persistent dynamic world modeling where dynamic subjects may leave and subsequently re-enter the camera field of view. Given textual prompt, an observed perspective prefix X0:K1, and -frame camera trajectory Cx with known intrinsics, the objective is to synthesize the remaining frames of the -frame perspective video X. Crucially, returning subjects must maintain identity consistency and plausible physical motion throughout the interval spent outside the viewport. OmniPersist addresses this task by jointly generating alongside temporally sparse panoramic video P. The panoramic stream captures scene evolution across all viewing directions, while the perspective stream adheres to the prescribed camera trajectory (see Fig. 1). Both streams share single diffusion transformer backbone and exchange features via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) and Temporal Compensation (TemComp), as illustrated in Fig. 2. Both streams rely solely on the perspective prefix, text prompt, and camera parameters, without requiring any auxiliary depth, panoramic images, or video inputs. 3.2. When panoramic visualization is not explicitly required, only the perspective stream is decoded, incurring zero additional decoding overhead. 5 Dataset Construction. Unlike HyDRA [6], which constructs its training and evaluation sets within simulators (i.e., Unreal Engine 5) that exhibit limited visual realism, we curate our dataset directly from real-world environments. We construct paired panoramic and perspective videos by simulating camera viewing trajectories over panoramic footage from the 360-1M dataset [38]. Following the filtering protocols in Argus [24] and UCPE [60], 125K high-quality video clips are selected. Each clip consists of 81 frames at 16 fps, with perspective resolution of 832 480 and panoramic resolution of 1024 512. We design four distinct camera trajectory types: object tracking, single revisit, double revisit, and full camera rotation of 360, covering both continuous subject following and leave-and-revisit patterns. Perspective viewpoints retain the camera-center trajectory of the original panoramic video while dynamically varying the viewing orientation. The evaluation set contains 300 videos whose source footage is strictly excluded from the training split. Details of the construction pipeline are provided in the suppl. Implementation Details. Under the image-to-video (I2V) protocol, generation is conditioned on single perspective frame (K = 1), whereas the video continuation setting conditions on 21 frames (K = 21). Both settings target the generation of 81-frame videos. OmniPersist is implemented based on the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone [39]. We instantiate OmniPersist across two representative cameracontrol paradigms, applying rank-32 LoRA [14] to linear layers in the self-attention and feed-forward blocks. Under CameraCtrl [11], view-specific ray adapters inject the camera features of the two views into their respective input tokens. Under UCPE [60], camera-attention layers process both views according to their ray geometries under unified coordinate and scale reference. GeoAnch and TemComp are embedded after each DiT Block. All OmniPersist variants adopt mixed-interval sampling, uniformly drawing {1, 2, 4, 10} and prefix length {1, 21} per example. Using AdamW [23] with learning rate of 104 and total batch size of 8 on 8 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the UCPEand CameraCtrl-based variants converge in 20K and 80K iterations, respectively. During inference, all diffusion models employ 50 denoising steps. Some models are evaluated solely on I2V, due to incompatibility with video continuation tasks. Evaluation Protocol. We evaluate performance across 14 perspective-video metrics structured into four groups. (1) Overall visual quality is measured via FID [12], FVD [37], and center-crop FVD (FVDc). (2) Camera controllability is evaluated via rotation (Rot) and translation (Trans) errors [11], CamMC [46], and absolute trajectory error (ATE) on ViPE-reconstructed [15] poses anchored at frame zero. Following UCPE [60], predicted and reference translations are independently normalized by their maximum trajectory radius. (3) Background revisit fidelity is evaluated using PSNR, SSIM [45], and LPIPS [62] between generated and ground-truth frames at camera-selected revisit timestamps, masked by intersected static backgrounds. (4) Dynamic persistence is assessed via foreground DINOv2 [25] feature similarity for overall subject identity (ID) and re-entry identity (R-ID), visibility F1-score (Vis.), and normalized subject trajectory error (Traj.). These metrics evaluate whether dynamic subject successfully returns, retains its appearance, and follows the ground-truth trajectory (the latter being more informative for video continuation). Quantitative and Qualitative Results We adopt = 4 as the primary setting for both quantitative and qualitative evaluations. Quantitative Comparisons. As shown in Table 1, under the I2V task, OmniPersist consistently improves all 14 metrics over the respective baselines for both CameraCtrl [11] and UCPE [60]. Specifically, re-entry identity increases from 0.2325 to 0.3355 with CameraCtrl and from 0.2097 to 0.3694 with UCPE. Camera rotation and translation errors drop from 13.086 / 0.531 to 5.556 / 0.399 for CameraCtrl, and from 8.127 / 0.431 to 4.976 / 0.376 for UCPE. FVD under UCPE improves from 333.7 to 272.7. Notably, even when compared against larger released world models, including LiveWorld [8] (14B, which explicitly models multi-entity evolution by additional diffusion models) and LingBot-World 2.0 [10] (28B), the UCPE-based OmniPersist outperforms LiveWorld across all 14 metrics and surpasses LingBot-World 2.0 on 13 of the 14 metrics. As reported in Table 2, under the video continuation task, both variants again surpass their respective baselines across all 14 metrics. In particular, re-entry identity increases from 0.2494 to 0.3771 with CameraCtrl and from 0.2778 to 0.3849 with UCPE. Subject trajectory error decreases from 0.5161 to 0.4289 with CameraCtrl and from 0.5255 to 0.4245 with UCPE. Moreover, CameraCtrl-based OmniPersist improves background revisit PSNR by 1.79 dB and camera rotation error by 7.359. Both variants also outperform HyDRA [6], LiveWorld [8], Matrix-World 3.0 [47], and SANA-WM [64] across all 14 metrics. In summary, OmniPersist achieves consistent gains in overall visual quality, camera controllability, background revisit fidelity, and dynamic subject persistence across both generation tasks and camera control mechanisms. Qualitative Comparisons. Figure 3 demonstrates that OmniPersist maintains strong consistency for both static backgrounds and dynamic subjects across camera revisit. Specifically, the road layout and surrounding vegetation remain structurally coherent, while both pedestrians preserve their clothing details and recognizable appearances upon reentry. Compared with perspective-only baselines, our results better preserve both subjects and their continued walking motion after the camera returns. More qualitative results and panoramic visualization are provided in the suppl. 4.3. Ablation Studies We first isolate the contributions of panoramic evolution, GeoAnch, and TemComp using CameraCtrl [11] at = 4. We then analyze the effect of panoramic sampling density and evaluate the computational overhead of our framework. Effect of Joint Panoramic Evolution. As shown in Table 3, compared to the perspective-only baseline (w/o Pano), adding panoramic support (w/ Pano) improves reentry identity (R-ID) from 0.2325 to 0.3256 for I2V and from 0.2494 to 0.3167 for video continuation. However, visual quality degrades inconsistently without explicit crossview alignment: I2V FID worsens from 23.60 to 26.16, while video continuation FVD increases from 227.5 to 246.0. When explicit spatial and temporal coupling are incorporated, these scores improve substantially to 22.18 and 194.9, respectively. These results indicate that although the panoramic stream supplies essential information about returning subjects, naive joint modeling alone is insufficient to maintain generation quality. Effect of GeoAnch and TemComp. Adding GeoAnch improves all four camera-control and three background-revisit metrics over panoramic modeling alone (w/ Pano) in both tasks (see Table 3). Conclusion In this paper, we address the critical challenge of dynamic object persistence in camera-controlled world models, where out-of-view moving entities frequently mutate or vanish upon viewpoint revisits. To resolve this limitation, we present OmniPersist, single-stage framework that couples perspective video generation with 360 panoramic evolution within unified diffusion model, requiring no initial panoramic images or auxiliary models. By operating the panoramic stream at lower frame rate, OmniPersist efficiently supports plausible evolution of out-of-view content. We seamlessly bridge the two streams across space and time via Geometric Anchoring (GeoAnch) for synchronous spatial correspondence and Temporal Compensation (TemComp) for cross-frame temporal aggregation. Extensive experiments show that OmniPersist achieves consistent performance gains across both latent-level (CameraCtrl) and attention-level (UCPE) camera conditioning in visual fidelity, camera controllability, background revisit consistency, and dynamic persistence. Limitations and Future Work. While OmniPersist sustains dynamic persistence during inference without requiring panoramic inputs, its training currently relies on panoramic video data. Nevertheless, with the increasing prevalence of omnidirectional capture hardware and realistic 3D simulation platforms, high-quality panoramic video assets are expected to expand rapidly. In future work, we plan to extend this framework toward real-time streaming and long-horizon video generation, and investigate its applications in robotic navigation. 8 OmniPersist: Persistent Dynamic World Modeling via Coupled Panoramic Evolution

Sec. details the implementation of our framework. Sec. provides additional ablation studies, quantitative evaluations, and qualitative results. A. Dataset Construction A.1. Overview of the Pipeline curation pipeline Our converts high-resolution raw panoramic footage into synchronized pairs of equirectangular projection (ERP) and perspective video clips. The panoramic stream is standardized by downsampling the footage to resolution of 1024 512, with its camera-to-world poses calibrated using ViPE [15]. To simulate realistic camera viewing trajectories with intentional leave-and-revisit patterns, we ground camera motion on moving foreground subjects. Specifically, we employ SAM 3.1 [4] to track dynamic entities directly across the ERP frames. The initial camera orientation is anchored to reliably tracked subject exhibiting sufficient pixel area near the panoramic center, establishing stable visual prefix. If the subject is initially located off-center, we apply horizontal rotation to the panorama to bring it to the central meridian. Guided by the motion paths of tracked subjects, we synthesize four categories of camera trajectories: object tracking, single revisit, double revisit, and full 360 camera rotations. Perspective video clips are rendered from the panoramic footage along the generated viewing trajectories and scaled to resolution of 832 480. To preserve visual fidelity and respect source-resolution constraints, the horizontal field of view (FoV) is capped at maximum of 120, while the minimum horizontal FoV is restricted to ensure that the natively sampled resolution is no less than half of 832 480 (limiting upscaling to factor of two). The vertical FoV is determined by the 832 : 480 aspect ratio. The absolute camera pose of each perspective frame is computed by compounding the calibrated panoramic pose with the simulated relative viewport transformation. Specifically, at discrete frame index t, the camera-to-world poses satisfy the geometric relationship: Cx = Cp Vt, Cx , Cp , Vt R44, (A) 9 Table A. Camera trajectory programs. The ten parameterized programs are categorized into the four semantic trajectory types described in the main paper. Trajectory Type Notation Trajectory Pattern Object tracking Single revisit Ttrk Tsr,1 Tsr,2 Tsr,3 Tsr,4 Double revisit Tdr,1 Tdr,2 Tdr,3 Tdr,4 Full 360 rotation Trot Continuous subject tracking Horizontal pan and return Asymmetric turn with pitch tilt Vertical detour Return overshoot Double horizontal pan and return Double asymmetric turn with tilt Double vertical detour Double return overshoot 360 rotation where Cx denotes the absolute camera-to-world pose of the perspective frame, Cp represents the calibrated pose of the panoramic frame, and Vt is the homogeneous pure-rotation matrix governing the relative viewport orientation. Both pose sequences are defined in shared world coordinate system anchored to the coordinate frame of the initial perspective camera, such that V0 = I. Because Vt contains solely rotational components, it steers the perspective viewing direction while strictly preserving the optical center trajectory of the source panorama. Consequently, physical translations of the panoramic capture device are faithfully preserved in the perspective clips, whereas the rendering process introduces no artificial translational offsets or synthesized motion parallax, guaranteeing physically grounded perspective observations. A.2. Camera Trajectory Synthesis We synthesize perspective camera trajectories across four semantic categories, defined by ten parameterized programs as summarized in Table A. These categories include object tracking (Ttrk) as control baseline with continuous tracking, single revisit (Tsr,1...4) where the camera turns away from the subject once and returns, double revisit (Tdr,1...4) with two leave-and-return cycles, and full rotation (Trot) performing an approximately 360 panoramic turn. To generate smooth and realistic camera motion, each trajectory interpolates yaw, pitch, and roll keyframes using piecewise quintic Hermite splines, ensuring continuous angular velocity and acceleration. Crucially, the reference camera orientation dynamically follows the moving subject rather than remaining static in world coordinates. Camera offsets are added on top of this moving reference orientation. Consequently, when the camera returns, it points to the current position of the subject instead of resetting to the initial orientation at the start of the video. Single-revisit trajectories share an out-and-back structure with four motion patterns. Horizontal pan-and-return trajectories (Tsr,1) place the maximum yaw turn at the midpoint, producing symmetric departure and return phases. Asymmetric turns (Tsr,2) shift the peak turn away from the temporal midpoint and add small pitch tilt, producing unequal departure and return durations alongside vertical angle changes. Vertical detours (Tsr,3) combine the horizontal sweep with alternating positive and negative pitch waypoints, guiding the camera through an out-of-plane detour rather than flat path. Return overshoots (Tsr,4) swing the camera past the reference heading to the opposite side before correcting back to the target direction. Double revisits (Tdr,1...4) repeat this process twice, separating the two turns with brief pause. To avoid visual distortion during fast turns, we limit the maximum angular speed to 90/s for single revisits (Tsr), 105/s for double revisits (Tdr, Ttrk), and 120/s for full rotation (Trot). If planned trajectory exceeds these speed limits, pauses and transition times are adjusted. If the speed is still too high, the rotation angle is scaled down accordingly. A.3. Dataset Statistics Dataset Scale. The curated dataset comprises 125K training clips and 300 evaluation clips, with strictly disjoint source videos between the two splits. Multiple perspective clips are rendered from individual panoramic source videos under different camera trajectories. Across the dataset, the ten parameterized trajectory programs in Table are sampled uniformly, ensuring balanced representation. Camera Motion Direction Distribution. We analyze the distribution of camera motion directions across the training set to assess the diversity of generated camera paths. For each clip, the camera motion direction is computed from the net horizontal rotation between the first and last frames. As illustrated in Figure A(a), the motion directions span the complete 360 range with broad coverage. Because revisit trajectories where the camera returns toward the subject constitute major proportion of the dataset, the distribution naturally exhibits higher density around 0 and 180, while maintaining substantial representation across all lateral angles. Field of View Distribution. Figure A(b) illustrates the horizontal field of view (FoV) distribution across the training set. Because source panoramic videos vary in resolution and perspective sampling strictly enforces an upscaling limit, the resulting FoV distribution exhibits tiered density rather than strictly uniform spread. The distribution maintains substantial coverage across both standard viewing angles and wide-angle configurations. This broad FoV coverage prevents models from overfitting to fixed focal length and encourages generalization across diverse perspective geometries. B.
